snip.t: Good insight predicts better adherence and outcome; poor insight is typical of mania and psychosis.
Olfactory hallucination: Smelling odours that are not present; can be experienced in epilepsy, depression or psychosis.
Dopamine: Reward, motivation, movement, thinking — Excess activity in some pathways is linked to psychosis.
It is useful in depression, anxiety, OCD and psychosis.

Keep the alternatives open: a mood disorder with psychotic features (mania or depression), substance-induced psychosis (cannabis, khat, alcohol), and a medical or neurological cause (HIV, epilepsy, head injury, thyroid, delirium).
Mood symptoms: elevated or depressed mood before or during the psychosis.
Anosognosia: Unawareness or denial of illness or deficits; frequently encountered in psychosis and some neurological conditions.
Mesolimbic: Reward and salience — Positive symptoms of psychosis (hallucinations, delusions) — Positive symptoms improve (the aim of treatment)

qs.q: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus develops new-onset psychosis and depression. Which autoantibody has a strongly established odds ratio for these specific psychiatric manifestations?
qs.e: Anti-ribosomal-P antibodies carry a 4 to 10 times odds ratio for psychosis and depression in SLE patients. Other antibodies like anti-SCL-70 are typically associated with scleroderma rather than lupus-related psychiatric symptoms.

ai.title: Psychosis
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Psychosis is a clinical syndrome of loss of reality testing, presenting with hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized thinking. It requires rapid assessment of organic causes, safety, and initiation of antipsychotic therapy.

sections.p: Psychosis is defined by DSM‑5/ICD‑10 as a disturbance of thought content and perception that leads to impaired reality testing. Core features are hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized speech/behaviour. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale or PANSS if available.

t.b: Low Hb or high WBC suggests infection or chronic disease
Elevated transaminases with jaundice raise suspicion of hepatic cause
High creatinine limits use of certain antipsychotics

sections.p: Severity is graded by the Clinical Global Impression‑Severity (CGI‑S) and by the presence of self‑harm or violence. Staging follows the 5‑stage model: 1) prodrome, 2) first episode, 3) recurrent, 4) chronic, 5) residual. Early intervention improves prognosis.
b: Stage 1: subtle changes, Stage 5: residual symptoms

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the top differential includes: 1) Substance‑induced (khat, alcohol, cannabis), 2) HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder, 3) Tuberculosis meningitis, 4) Malaria cerebral, 5) Hepatitis B/C, 6) Thyroid dysfunction, 7) Schistosomiasis, 8) Herbal toxins, 9) Delirium from infection or metabolic derangement, 10) Primary psychotic disorders.

Patients may report hearing voices, seeing things, or having fixed beliefs. Behaviour can be agitated, catatonic, or disorganised. Safety concerns include self‑harm, aggression, or wandering. Physical exam may reveal tremor, dysarthria, or signs of infection.
Prioritise tests that are available locally and that can rule out treatable causes. When a test is unavailable, use clinical judgment and empirical treatment.

t.b: CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis and high protein indicates TB or viral
Low TSH suggests hyperthyroidism, high TSH hypothyroidism
Positive for cannabinoids or alcohol metabolites

sections.p: Urgent red flags: suicidal ideation, homicidal thoughts, severe agitation, seizures, or signs of intracranial pressure. Complications include self‑harm, malnutrition, infections from wandering, and medication toxicity.

Treat the underlying cause first. Provide a safe environment, monitor vitals, and start antipsychotic therapy. First‑line agents are low‑dose haloperidol or olanzapine if available. Avoid drugs with anticholinergic or QT‑prolonging effects in patients with cardiac or hepatic disease.

After acute stabilization, arrange outpatient follow‑up, psychoeducation, and adherence support. Screen for substance use and HIV regularly. Vaccinate against hepatitis B and provide malaria prophylaxis where appropriate.
Delirium, dementia, mood disorder with psychotic features, epilepsy, and substance intoxication/withdrawal.
Normal CBC can miss early HIV; normal electrolytes can miss subtle hyponatraemia; normal TSH may miss central hypothyroidism. Clinical context is essential.
b: Early HIV may have normal CD4
Hyponatraemia can be mild and missed

faq.q: What is the most common cause of psychosis in East Africa?
faq.a: Substance use (khat, alcohol, cannabis) and HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder are the leading causes.

faq.q: Which antipsychotic is safest in a patient with hepatic impairment?
faq.a: Haloperidol is preferred because it has minimal hepatic metabolism and can be given IM or IV.

faq.q: How do you differentiate delirium from psychosis?
faq.a: Delirium has fluctuating consciousness, impaired attention, and a reversible cause; psychosis has intact consciousness and fixed false beliefs.

exam: A 24‑year‑old presents with auditory hallucinations and agitation. What is the first step? — Assess safety, rule out infection (malaria, TB), and start low‑dose haloperidol.
A patient with known HIV develops visual hallucinations. What investigation is most urgent? — Lumbar puncture to rule out TB meningitis.
Why is chlorpromazine avoided in a patient with a history of epilepsy? — It lowers the seizure threshold.
A patient reports hearing voices that say they are being watched. Which symptom is most characteristic of schizophrenia? — Delusions of persecution.
What is the key difference between psychosis and mood disorder with psychotic features? — Presence of mood symptoms (elevated or depressed mood) in the latter.
A patient with psychosis is refusing medication. What strategy improves adherence? — Psychoeducation and involving family in care.
